messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Interior Designer
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Anniversaries: The anniversary of the event, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones, Funerals/Graves: Funerals, cemeteries, or grief-related events
  Maladaptive Strategies: Worst Case Rehearsal: mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arjun Mehta was 39 when his older sister died without warning. She had collapsed at home and was gone before the ambulance arrived. In the first stunned days after the call, what lodged in him most sharply was not only the fact of her death but the atmosphere around it: the funeral home, the smell of flowers, the sight of mourners speaking in hushed voices about who had been lost and who was left behind. He remembered standing near the casket feeling unreal, as if the scene were happening at a distance and directly inside his body at the same time. Since then, grief-related settings have carried a particular force for him. A funeral, a cemetery, even a conversation about someone losing a parent or sibling can pull him back toward that first week.

Over the months that followed, Arjun tried to get on with work and family life. He is an interior designer, and much of his day is spent meeting clients, visiting homes, and discussing personal spaces with people who often disclose intimate details about marriages, illnesses, aging parents, and deaths in the family. He has found that when a client casually mentions bereavement while explaining why they want to redo a bedroom or clear out a relative’s belongings, his stomach clenches before he has fully registered what was said. Around the anniversary of his sister’s death, this reaction intensifies. He starts tracking the date weeks in advance and becomes preoccupied with how bad it might be this year, running through images of himself falling apart at work, losing control in front of clients, or getting trapped in the same helpless shock he felt when she died.

Those moments do not stay as thoughts for long. When he passes a cemetery while driving to a job site or receives an invitation to a memorial service, he can suddenly feel as if the original loss is happening again. His chest tightens, his arms go cold, and for a moment he is back in the funeral home, braced for news that cannot be changed. He says his body “goes there” before his mind catches up. By the time he realizes he is only hearing someone talk about a death or seeing headstones from the road, he is already flooded and on edge. At home, his wife has noticed that after these episodes he is quick to snap over small things, especially if she asks what is wrong when he is trying to steady himself.

Because those reactions feel so immediate and uncontrollable, Arjun has built his life around trying to stay ahead of them. As the anniversary approaches, he becomes absorbed in mentally rehearsing the worst possible versions of the day, telling himself that if he imagines every way it could undo him, he will be less blindsided. He avoids putting the date on the calendar, declines family plans that might acknowledge it, and tries to keep himself busy with site visits and vendor calls so he does not have to sit with any reminder of his sister. He has also started steering away from grief-related events altogether. If he learns that a client meeting will include discussion of a recently deceased relative, he will try to shorten the visit or redirect the conversation back to fabrics, lighting, anything practical.

Yet these efforts have not given him the sense of control he wants. The more he rehearses catastrophe, the more vivid and near it feels, and the more watchful he becomes for signs that he is about to lose himself in it. Avoiding anniversaries has made the date feel more dangerous, not less; each year it seems to arrive with greater dread. Keeping away from funerals and other reminders has left him less able to tolerate the ordinary ways loss comes up in adult life, so even brief mention of someone else’s bereavement can set off the same jolt in his body. Afterward he grows irritable, ashamed of how harshly he has spoken, and even more determined to avoid anything that might trigger another episode.

What finally brought Arjun to treatment was a scene at work this past year. During a consultation, a client explained that she was renovating after her mother’s death. Before he could respond, he felt himself drop into that old sense that the loss was happening now; his heart pounded, his hands shook, and he had to excuse himself to the restroom. He later barked at an assistant who asked if he was all right. He came home frightened by how little control he seemed to have and admitted to his wife that he had been arranging his life around not being reminded of his sister. What frightens him most is that grief has become something ambush-like and dangerous, waiting in dates, conversations, and places he cannot fully avoid. What he hopes for, cautiously, is to remember his sister without feeling as though he is being thrown back into the moment of losing her.
